I can find surprisingly little information on this guy outside of a small guide on homebrewing and distilling in northern climes, The Alaskan Bootlegger's Bible. But considering that I've seen pictures of an Alaskan labor commissioner with a marijuana plant in his office during the 70s, I'm pretty inclined to believe his account. Engels operated his winery from 1958 to 1986. Oddly enough, several communities passed laws affecting the transportation of alcohol in 1986.

Alaska has had many colorful characters, but few can match Father Emmett Engel, The bootlegging priest. Until his death in 1986, the fiery Father defiantly operated a illegal milk winery at Big Lake, Alaska and pursued his dream of of establishing his Casa de San José monastery. Father Engel was quite a man, a retired priest from the Diocese at Whitehorse, Yukon Territory. He professed to follow a divine directive to produce his milk wine and not only ignored and defied secular laws which interfered with his mission, but on occasion was known to tap a trooper on his snot locker.

He derived his inspiration from a visit from the Holy Mother when he was 28 years old. He was told through another priest that he must make wine from whey. He quotes her as saying, "I have chosen this young man which contains no fusel oil. I choose it as my own wine." Father Engel explained that the Devil reigns unchallenged in alcohol containing fusel oils, but without them, favorable effects would follow. Interestingly enough, the BATF tests of Father Engels product showed fusel oils present, but only in minute amounts. The good Father did not accept the lab's conclusion.

Now Father Engels was not our run-of-the-mill, sneak in the night bootlegger. Heaven's No! He had an enormous yellow sign out on the Parks Highway proclaiming his milk winery. He put out flyers saying:

Engel wine! Super Fine! No Hangover! Yes, moon over! Wine four years old! Much different!

He gave authorities fits and ulcers. One enforcement official said that in 32 years if service, Engel was "the most difficult person I have ever dealt with." When the cops and revenuers raided him for everything from licenses, to taxes, and sanitation, the good Father apparently lacked tact, using phrases like "where are your cloven hooves? Where is your tail?" and calling the troopers "Roman soldiers." When verbal communications failed, Father Engel apparently reverted to nonverbal communications and on at least one occasion, "kicked ass" on a raiding party of revenuers and troopers sent to confiscate four barrels of his product. The case was settled in a local court with a fine of $500 over the protests of authorities who apparently well over $500 dollars worth of nonverbal communication. The good Father continued making and selling wine.

It was good wine. I bought it and drank it. Maybe the dogs did pee on the dried milk sacks occasionally. I don't doubt that mouse turds and the occasional mouse found its way into the vats. Adds body. Father Engel was not one to get along with authority, a bit eccentric even by his own admission, "I'm unusual, even to myself." But he made a good and wholesome milk wine with a motive that warrants thought, not ridicule. It was honey colored wine, hard to define or describe. It had a full body, not like a fruit wine, not quite like a sake either. It had a different, this is wholesome and good for me taste. When Father Engel Left, he seems to have taken his recipe with him. The recipes which follow are not so divinely inspired, but when you try them, do so in memory of Father Emmett Engel, the wine making priest.
